title: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: During the growth of an individual snowflake its shape should alternate between tree-like and faceted forms, as new branches grow and then collide with one another.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: one expects that during the growth of a particular snowflake there should be alternation between tree-like and faceted shapes, as new branches grow but then collide with each other.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “The Growth of Crystals” (from p. 369), p. 371. Scope: time course of individual snowflake growth

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-03: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction maps cleanly to time-resolved shape measurements and collision events. However, broad open datasets of individual snowflakes throughout growth with controlled conditions are not readily available. New controlled time-lapse observations are needed for a decisive test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Segment time-lapse images of individual snowflakes, classify each frame by branchiness and faceting, and test for repeated ordered transitions associated with branch collisions. Persistent monotonic morphology or transitions unrelated to collisions would refute the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public collections emphasize final crystals rather than complete growth trajectories.

Temperature and supersaturation changes can independently drive morphology transitions.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is a specific time order, which is sharper than a static resemblance. Laboratory growth records exist but are scattered and rarely cover a full crystal from seed to completion under constant conditions. Those records can test the prediction for some habits and not for snowflake growth in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score time-lapse records of individual snowflakes for switches between branched and faceted outline as growth proceeds. Repeated alternation within single crystals would support the prediction; steady habit, or switches that track only external temperature changes, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
External changes in humidity can mimic an intrinsic growth-and-collision cycle.

Most public images are finished crystals, so the time order of tree-like and faceted stages is often missing.
